questions.stem: According to the foundational terminologies in immunology presented in the lecture, how is an "antigen" defined?
options: A serum enzyme produced by activated neutrophils during acute inflammation
A substance capable of stimulating the human immune system to produce an immune response
A specialized antibody class found exclusively in mucosal epithelial secretions
A cell surface receptor expressed only on mature CD8+ T-lymphocytes
questions.explanation: An antigen is defined as any substance capable of stimulating the human immune system to produce a specific immune response against it.

questions.stem: In 1939, A. Tiselius subjected blood serum to electrophoresis and demonstrated that antibodies reside within which specific protein fraction?
options: Albumin fraction
Alpha-globulin fraction
Beta-globulin fraction
Gamma-globulin fraction
questions.explanation: Electrophoresis separates serum proteins into albumin, alpha, beta, and gamma globulins. Tiselius demonstrated that antibodies are located in the gamma-globulin fraction, earning them the name immunoglobulins.

questions.stem: According to the cellular development classification of the immune system, what percentage of circulating white blood cells is represented by agranular leukocytes (plasma cells, T/B/NK lymphocytes, monocytes, and dendritic cells)?
questions.explanation: Leukocytes in circulation are categorized as granular or agranular. Agranular leukocytes make up 35% of circulating immune cells and include monocytes, plasma cells, dendritic cells, and lymphocytes (T, B, NK).

questions.stem: By what precise mechanism do Natural Killer (NK) cells selectively eliminate unhealthy or virus-infected target cells during immunological surveillance?
options: Secreting dimeric IgA antibodies across epithelial basolateral membranes
Using perforins to form transmembrane pores and granzymes to initiate apoptosis
Producing high concentrations of hydrochloric acid inside the phagolysosome
Converting serum fibrinogen into cross-linked insoluble fibrin threads
questions.explanation: NK cells recognize unhealthy target cells (expressing abnormal or viral proteins) and release perforin (which forms a transmembrane pore) and granzymes (which enter through the pore to trigger programmed cell death / apoptosis via gene expression).

questions.stem: Which of the following is explicitly listed as one of the three cardinal features of the adaptive immune system?
options: Absence of immunological memory
Memory (exposure enhances the ability to respond faster and larger to subsequent challenges)
Instantaneous onset with zero time lag
Non-specific action against all foreign particles equally
questions.explanation: The cardinal features of adaptive immunity are Specificity, Diversity, and Memory. Immunological memory ensures that subsequent exposures to the same antigen yield a faster, larger secondary immune response.

questions.stem: What is the basic molecular structure and polypeptide chain composition of a monomeric immunoglobulin molecule?
options: A single polypeptide chain with a molecular weight of 25,000 Da
A Y-shaped heterodimer composed of two identical light (L) chains (25 kDa each) and two identical heavy (H) chains (50 kDa or more each)
A pentameric ring of ten light chains linked by disulfide bridges
Four identical heavy chains bound to a central secretory component
questions.explanation: An antibody is a Y-shaped heterodimer consisting of four polypeptide chains: two identical light chains (MW ~25,000 Da each) and two identical heavy chains (MW ~50,000 Da or more each), joined by disulfide bonds and noncovalent interactions.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin class constitutes approximately 75–85% of total serum antibodies, has a half-life of 23 days, and possesses the unique ability to cross the placenta?
options: IgM
IgA
IgG
IgE
questions.explanation: IgG represents 75–85% of total serum antibodies, has the longest half-life (23 days), possesses two paratopes, acts against bacteria and viruses, and crosses the placenta to confer natural passive immunity to the fetus and neonate.

questions.stem: What is the specific structural function of the "Secretory Component" attached to dimeric IgA in mucosal secretions?
options: It initiates the classical complement cascade
It protects IgA from denaturation by bacterial proteases produced by intestinal flora
It binds to Fc receptors on mast cells to trigger immediate histamine degranulation
It binds directly to oxygen molecules to transport them across mucosal membranes
questions.explanation: Dimeric secretory IgA consists of two monomeric units joined by a J-chain and wrapped in a secretory component (derived from epithelial poly-Ig receptors). The secretory component shields IgA from destruction by bacterial proteases in the gut lumen.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin class is the largest in size (MW ~900 kDa, existing mostly as a pentamer bound by a J-chain), appears first during a primary infection, and cannot cross the placenta?
options: IgD
IgA
IgM
IgE
questions.explanation: IgM is the largest antibody (MW 900 kDa), constructed of 5 or 6 units (mostly pentamers) bound by a J-chain. It is the first antibody to appear in response to initial antigen exposure, fixes complement, acts as an opsonin, and cannot cross the placenta.

questions.stem: Which antibody class is present in the lowest serum concentration (0.019%), has the shortest half-life (2.5 days), is uniquely heat-labile (inactivated at 56°C in 1 hour), and mediates Type I hypersensitivity?
options: IgG
IgD
IgE
IgM
questions.explanation: IgE has the lowest serum concentration (0.019%), shortest half-life (2.5 days), is the only heat-labile antibody (inactivated at 56°C for 1 hour), exhibits homocytotropism for mast cell/basophil Fc receptors, and drives Type I allergic hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: What is the established physiological function of Immunoglobulin D (IgD)?
options: Direct opsonization of encapsulated bacteria in intravascular spaces
Acting as a membrane-bound B-cell receptor alongside IgM on the surface of B cells
Neutralizing viral enterotoxins within the lumen of the small intestine
Crossing the placental barrier during the third trimester of pregnancy
questions.explanation: IgD is found as membrane Ig on the surface of B cells, functioning as a B-cell antigen receptor alongside monomeric IgM. It has the highest carbohydrate content among immunoglobulins and no other known effector function.

questions.stem: Which set of characteristics distinguishes a Primary Immune Response from a Secondary (Anamnestic) Immune Response?
options: Primary response has a short lag phase and produces massive high-titer IgG
Primary response is slow, sluggish, and short-lived with a long lag phase, producing low titers dominated by IgM
Primary response produces high-titer antibodies that persist for decades
Primary response relies exclusively on memory T-lymphocytes
questions.explanation: The primary response is slow, sluggish, and short-lived, featuring a long lag phase, low antibody titers that do not persist, and IgM as the primary antibody. The secondary response is prompt, powerful, prolonged, features a negligible lag phase, and is dominated by high-titer IgG.

questions.stem: How is passive immunization distinguished from active immunization regarding its duration of effect and acquisition mechanism?
options: Passive immunization provides permanent protection by generating memory B and T cells
Passive immunization involves transferring preformed antibodies (maternal or antitoxins) and provides temporary protection
Active immunization is acquired exclusively through intravenous injection of preformed animal sera
Active immunization fails to stimulate T and B lymphocyte proliferation
questions.explanation: Passive immunization transfers preformed antibodies (naturally via placenta/milk or artificially via antitoxins/immune globulins), offering immediate but temporary protection without memory cell formation. Active immunization (via infection or vaccines) stimulates T/B cells to form memory cells, providing relatively permanent immunity.

questions.stem: Which cluster of differentiation (CD) markers is specifically associated with B-lymphocytes and humoral immunity in the comparison diagrams?
options: CD4 and CD8
CD19 and CD20
CD2 and CD3
CD16 and CD56
questions.explanation: B-cells mature in the bone marrow, mediate humoral immunity, and express markers such as CD19, CD20, CD22, CD40, CD80, and CD86. T-cells mature in the thymus and express CD4+ and CD8+ for cell-mediated immunity.

questions.stem: What is the primary diagnostic principle underlying Latex Agglutination tests in clinical serology?
options: Photon emission triggered by enzyme-substrate reactions
Visible clumping occurring when antibodies bind to target antigens coated onto inert polystyrene latex particles
UV light visualization of fluorescently-labeled spirochetes
Electrophoretic separation of serum into four distinct globulin bands
questions.explanation: In latex agglutination tests (such as CRP testing or bacterial serotyping), visible clumping occurs when specific antibodies react with target antigens attached to the surface of inert polystyrene latex beads.

questions.stem: Which diagnostic serological technique uses fluorescently-labeled antibodies viewed under a specialized microscope and is commonly applied for Antinuclear Antibody (ANA) testing in systemic lupus erythematosus?
options: Chemiluminescence Immunoassay (CLIA)
Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR) test
Immunofluorescence Assay (IFA)
Radial Immunodiffusion (RID)
questions.explanation: Immunofluorescence Assay (IFA) utilizes fluorophore-labeled antibodies to visualize antigen location in tissues or cells under a fluorescence microscope. Key applications include ANA testing for lupus and direct detection of respiratory viruses.

questions.stem: What is the operational principle and primary advantage of Chemiluminescence Immunoassays (CLIA) in diagnostic serology?
options: Measures radioactive isotope decay to count target molecules
Combines antigen-antibody binding with chemical reactions that emit light, offering exceptionally high sensitivity and easy automation
Uses heat at 56°C to denature competing non-specific proteins
Measures bacterial growth rates in liquid broth over 14 days
questions.explanation: CLIA combines antigen-antibody reactions with light-emitting chemical markers. When a target analyte binds, a chemical reaction triggers photon emission strictly proportional to the analyte concentration, providing high sensitivity and automated throughput.

questions.stem: When analyzing paired serum samples (acute and convalescent sera) from a patient, what finding confirms a recent active infection?
options: A stable, unchanged IgG antibody titer across both samples drawn 3 weeks apart
A fourfold or greater rise in IgG antibody titer between acute and convalescent samples
Complete absence of serum IgM combined with a normal white blood cell count
A single positive nontreponemal RPR test result
questions.explanation: Demonstrating a fourfold (or greater) rise in specific IgG antibody titer between an acute-phase serum sample and a convalescent-phase sample (drawn 2–3 weeks later) confirms a recent active infection.

questions.stem: Which chemical factors present in saliva and tear secretions contribute to the chemical barriers of innate immunity?
options: Perforins, granzymes, and memory immunoglobulins
Lysozyme, peroxidase, and lactoferrin
Histamine, bradykinin, and leukotriene B4
Coagulation factors II, VII, and X
questions.explanation: Antimicrobial chemical factors present in saliva, tears, and secretions include lysozyme (cleaves bacterial peptidoglycan), peroxidase, and lactoferrin (sequesters iron), serving as the first line of innate defense.

questions.stem: What is the correct chronological sequence of intracellular events during phagocytosis by leukocytes following initial receptor binding?
options: Phagolysosome formation → Phagosome formation → Exocytosis
Phagosome formation → Fusion with lysosome to form phagolysosome → Intracellular killing and exocytosis of soluble debris
Exocytosis → Phagosome formation → Receptor clustering
Perforin pore formation → Granzyme release → Apoptosis
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis follows a step-by-step sequence: (1) receptor binding, (2) engulfment into a phagosome, (3) fusion with a lysosome to form a phagolysosome, (4) intracellular killing via enzymes/ROS/NO, and (5) exocytosis of soluble debris.
